claims.text: The patient presented with severe left knee pain and functional limitation due to end-stage osteoarthritis, characterized by a constant dull ache with episodes of sharp pain (8/10 to 9/10 severity) worsening over the last 12 months, exacerbated by walking, standing, and climbing stairs, with associated occasional swelling and stiffness but no radiation, redness, fever, or systemic symptoms.

Past medical history is significant for end-stage osteoarthritis of the left knee with no other significant conditions; family history includes maternal type 2 diabetes and paternal hypertension, with no family history of osteoarthritis or joint disorders.

Social history indicates the patient lives with parents, is independent in activities of daily living but requires assistance for prolonged walking or standing, is a non-smoker, consumes approximately 4 units of alcohol weekly, and has no recreational drug use.

Pre-operative examination on 20/12/25 revealed significant left knee deformity with valgus alignment, tenderness along the medial joint line, reduced range of motion with pain on flexion beyond 70 degrees, and mild effusion, with no signs of erythema, warmth, or active infection.

Pre-operative investigations on 20/12/25 showed mild anaemia with haemoglobin of 11.3 g/dL, while full blood count (excluding haemoglobin), urea and electrolytes, liver function tests, C-reactive protein, urinalysis, and ECG were all within normal limits.
The patient has no known drug or environmental allergies.
Ferrous sulfate 200 mg once daily was prescribed on 20/12/25 to address mild anaemia, with advice to increase dietary intake of iron-rich foods.

Anaesthetic assessment on 20/12/25 confirmed an ASA grade of I, with a Mallampati score of I, adequate mouth opening, normal thyromental distance, and no history of respiratory disease or anaesthetic complications in the family.

Formal written consent for total left knee replacement was obtained on 21/12/25 after discussion of benefits, risks, and recovery expectations, with instructions to fast from midnight prior to surgery and avoid ibuprofen.

On admission on 05/01/26, the patient was alert and cooperative with stable vital signs (HR 74 bpm, BP 122/78 mmHg, RR 14 br/min, Temp 36.7°C, SpO2 98%), and the left knee showed gross deformity consistent with end-stage OA without erythema, warmth, or effusion.

Total left knee replacement was performed on 05/01/26 under general anaesthesia, revealing severe cartilage degeneration and subchondral bone exposure with no peri-articular inflammation or infection, resulting in the implantation of a cemented total knee prosthesis with minimal blood loss and no complications.

Intra-operative prophylaxis included Cefuroxime 1.5g IV, and post-operative care initiated in the PACU included Tinzaparin 4,500 units subcutaneously once daily for thromboprophylaxis and a PCA pump with IV morphine for pain management.

On 05/01/26, the patient reported moderate pain (6/10) at rest and with movement; the surgical site was clean with minimal serous drainage and no signs of infection, leading to a plan to start Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously once daily, Paracetamol 1g every 6 hours regularly, and Codeine phosphate 30 mg PRN for breakthrough pain.

Initial physiotherapy on 06/01/26 focused on gentle mobilisation, achieving 40 degrees of knee flexion with mild discomfort (VAS 4/10), with instructions for independent exercises twice daily and deep breathing exercises.
The GP was contacted on 06/01/26 to update on post-operative progress, with an anticipated discharge date of 09/01/26.

On 06/01/26, the patient reported mild pain well controlled with oral analgesia, with a clean and dry surgical site, no signs of infection or DVT, and stable vital signs (HR 78, BP 118/72, RR 16, Temp 36.8, SpO2 98%).

Physiotherapy on 07/01/26 involved walking a short distance with a Zimmer frame and assisted knee flexion/extension exercises, with the patient reporting mild discomfort (3/10) and tolerating the session well.
A pharmacist review on 07/01/26 recommended switching from IV to oral Paracetamol 1g QDS and continuing Ibuprofen 400mg TDS if tolerated.

Occupational therapy on 07/01/26 assessed activities of daily living, noting the patient maintained good balance with verbal prompts but required guidance to protect the operated knee, leading to recommendations for a raised toilet seat and sock aid.

On 07/01/26, the patient had a haemoglobin of 108 g/L indicating mild post-operative anaemia, was mobilising with a walking frame with improving gait, and the plan included Ferrous sulfate 200 mg BD and oral Ibuprofen 400 mg TDS.

On 08/01/26, the patient had satisfactory pain control and was mobilising effectively with a Zimmer frame; the plan included switching Paracetamol to PRN dosing, prescribing Co-amoxiclav 500/125 mg TDS for 7 days for wound infection prophylaxis, and continuing Ferrous sulfate 200 mg BD.
Final physiotherapy on 08/01/26 focused on crutch use for independent mobilisation, including walking on flat surfaces and navigating stairs, with the patient deemed safe for discharge with crutches.

Discharge planning on 08/01/26 included wound care instructions, a pain management regimen of oral Paracetamol 1g QDS and Ibuprofen 400mg TDS, and a follow-up appointment scheduled for 15/01/26 with the GP.

Occupational therapy review on 08/01/26 confirmed the patient demonstrated independence and safety in bed transfers, crutch use on stairs, and household tasks, with a home exercise programme provided and discharge planned for the following day.
